chapter_theme: Amuri dharana (அமுரிதாரணை): a water held within the body, called the drinking-water of strength and Siva-water, is praised as a medicine without rival. Drunk, alone or with pepper, gooseberry, turmeric and neem, it is said to make the body golden and supple, restore the hair, end grey hair and wrinkles and keep Yama away; Nandi taught it as a medicine of light that cannot be told.
structure_note: The water is introduced (845), its effects on body and mind praised (846 to 849), and its names and source in Nandi's teaching given last (850). The verses never name the water plainly; they call it குடிநீர், சிவநீர், சிவத்தின் நீர் and கானல் உவரி.

845.reading: The strengthening water that lies in the body is like a well-sweep set to draw from the sea; if one draws it by the one way in the body for the one purpose, life is spared distress and can seek its end.
845.nuance: அமுரி in the title is commonly taken as the body's own urine, and the chapter as a teaching on drinking it (amaroli); some readers take the water symbolically as the nectar of yoga. The sea and small well-sweep may mean the supply is ample beside the small draw, but the image is not explained. ஒருவழி ஒன்றுக்கு (one way, for one thing) is compressed, and உயிர் நாடலும் may mean 'life can seek' or 'one can attain life'.

846.reading: If one drinks this clarifying Siva-water, within a year the body shines without any defect; with breath held in the eight the mind too subsides, and the body, giving joy, becomes gold.
846.nuance: சிவநீர் (Siva-water) is the chapter's reverent name for the water. வளியுறும் எட்டின் is obscure: the eight may be the eight limbs of yoga or a measure of breath. காயம் கனகம் (the body as gold) is the alchemists' image of the perfected, undecaying body.

847.reading: Siva's water taken with a hundred peppercorns has no medicine to rival it; if people understand it and apply it to the crown of the head, the hair changes and grows anew.
847.nuance: மாறும் opens two lines in different senses: a rival (no medicine rivals this) and change (the hair changes). நுகரும் may mean the water is drunk with the pepper or that pepper is steeped in it; the verse doesn't say which. மறுமயிர் is read as new hair.

848.reading: Witless people say the salt water of the shore, near the bank, is to be avoided; for those who can drink it with the froth and scum removed, grey hair and wrinkles change, and Yama is not there either.
848.nuance: கானல் உவரி (brackish water of the shore) is taken as the same water under a disguising name; வரைவரை is read as 'avoid it, avoid it'. நரைதிரை (grey hair and wrinkles) and நமன் (Yama) make the promise one of youth and deathlessness, as in the body-perfecting chapters of this tantra.

849.reading: O you with curling hair and fair forehead, a wonder: if pepper, gooseberry, turmeric and neem are put into this water mixed with the hidden body, the body grows supple and the head grows dark.
849.nuance: The address to a woman (அளக நன்னுதலாய்) is taken in the tradition as Siva speaking to Shakti, or as a conventional address. களவு காயம் is obscure: காயம் may be the body or a spice such as asafoetida, and களவு 'hidden' or a corrupt word. இருளும் கபாலம் (the skull darkens) is read as the hair turning black. A variant gives இளகிடு for இளகும், with no change of sense.

850.reading: Nandi in his grace called it the hero's medicine, the gods' medicine and the woman's medicine; those who know it as the primal medicine know that across the wide earth this medicine of light cannot be told.
850.nuance: The names are given without explanation; நாரி மருந்து (woman's medicine) is unclear, perhaps tied to Shakti. The closing line can mean the medicine is too great for words or that it is not to be told openly, a secret teaching; both stand.

links.note: Both promise the end of grey hair and wrinkles (நரைதிரை) from a bodily practice: 727 from breath held at fixed hours, 848 from drinking the shore-water the witless shun.

The Naladiyar treats grey hair as certain to come, so the wise renounce in childhood; Tirumular says that for those who drink this water grey hair and wrinkles change and Yama is absent. The conflict holds if 848 is read literally of the body, not as a figure for spiritual youth.

845 says that drawing the body's own water 'by the one way, for the one purpose' spares life distress (நடலைப் படாது உயிர்). 724 gives the principle behind it: if the body perishes the life perishes, so 'I nurtured the body and nurtured life' (உடம்பை வளர்த்தேன் உயிர்வளர்த்தேனே). 845 is one of the means of nurture that 724 says he learned.

846 promises that drinking the Siva-water makes the body faultless within a year and turns it to gold (காயம் கனகமதாமே). Thiruppugazh 815 calls the body a filthy hut that perishes faster than a water-bubble and confesses he desired it and kept trying worthless medicines and many yogas (சாரமில் அவுடதமும் பல யோகமும்) until his mind cried 'enough'. One verse offers a body-perfecting medicine; the other renounces such medicines as futile and seeks only the feet.

847 says Siva's water with a hundred peppercorns (நூறு மிளகு) has no rival as medicine and, applied to the crown, makes the hair grow anew (மறுமயிராமே). 849 extends the recipe, adding gooseberry, turmeric and neem to the pepper (மிளகு நெல்லியும் மஞ்சளும் வேம்பு), and gives the same result on the head: the skull darkens (இருளும் கபாலம்). Together they show the chapter building one remedy for the hair, step by step.

850 names the Siva-water the hero's, the gods' and the primal medicine (ஆதி மருந்து) and says this medicine of light cannot be told. Naladiyar 132 says that in no world is there a medicine like learning for cutting away delusion (கல்விபோல் மம்மர் அறுக்கும் மருந்து). Both claim a matchless medicine, one for the body's decay, the other for the mind's confusion.
